citation: Lin, Xiao Ping, Bin Bin Li, Zhen Ning Yao, Zhi Yang, and Minshu Zhang. "The Impact of Virtual Reality on Student Engagement in the Classroom: A Critical Review of the Literature." Frontiers in Psychology 15 (2024): 1360574. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1360574.
discipline: educational psychology / educational technology -- PRISMA-informed critical literature review synthesizing 33 articles on VR and classroom student engagement
thesis: Lin, Li, Yao, Yang, and Zhang determine virtual reality's (VR) impact on student engagement in the classroom, defined via Wang and Degol's (2014) tripartite model of cognitive (attention, comprehension, retention), behavioral (attendance, participation), and affective (motivation, passion, learning efficacy) engagement. Three questions guide the review: (1) VR's positive impacts on education; (2) VR's challenges; (3) interventions addressing those challenges. Framed as a 'critical review' in Grant and Booth's (2009) sense -- a method that 'presents, analyses and synthesizes material from diverse sources' -- the paper synthesizes 33 PRISMA-screened articles (2014-2023) via a three-phase Google/Scopus/Elsevier keyword search plus reference-mining, rather than reporting new primary data. Boredom is never named anywhere in the paper (confirmed by direct text search); the operative vocabulary is exclusively 'engagement' (cognitive/behavioral/affective), 'motivation,' and 'digital literacy.'

sections.title: Title/Abstract/Keywords
sections.summary: Structured abstract (Objective/Methods/Results/Conclusion); previews the tripartite engagement model and headline findings (positive VR impact on engagement; system-pace, digital-literacy, and teacher-proficiency challenges).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: VR's 'three pillars' of presence, interactivity, and immersion (Lee et al. 2017); frames engagement via Wang and Degol (2014); adoption-rate claims (up to 96% of UK universities; Harvard VR labs); states the three guiding research questions.

sections.title: Method -- Searching strategy; Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sections.summary: Three-phase Google/Scopus/Elsevier keyword search, English-language, Jan.2014-Dec.2023, narrowing 97->63->20 articles via screening plus 13 manually reference-mined articles, N=33 final; PRISMA-based screening (Moher et al. 2009; Figure 1).

sections.title: Result -- Table 1 and citation-count discussion
sections.summary: Table 1 lists all 33 reviewed articles with inclusion rationale; notes rising annual publication trend (2014-2023); Wang and Degol (2014) most-cited (450); states explicit limitations (small literature base, only three databases, recency bias, generalizability caveat).

sections.title: The positive impact of VR on education
sections.summary: Three subsections tracking the tripartite model: cognitive engagement, behavioral engagement (with an internal pro/con debate), and affective engagement.

sections.title: The challenge of VR in education
sections.summary: Educational-system pace, student digital-literacy demands, and teacher VR-proficiency gaps, followed by a proposed solution (teacher training, via Alfalah 2018).

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates the positive-impact and challenge findings; calls on policymakers to fund teacher training and technical support.

sections.title: Author contributions; Funding; Conflict of interest; Correction note; Acknowledgments; Publisher's note; References
sections.summary: Hunan Province self-funded grant (MZ, principal investigator); notes a 2025 correction to the article (details not present in the extracted text).

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: core, source-native construct: 'engagement' (cognitive/behavioral/affective, Wang and Degol 2014) organizes the entire positive-impact section and the paper's structured abstract; the cross-walk from this cluster's boredom-contrast label to the review's own engagement vocabulary is still this entry's own mapping, since the source cites no flow theory and never opposes engagement to boredom or monotony

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: thin, single-line treatment: Table 1 credits Misak (2018) only as an 'introduction to VR improves students' meta-cognition,' never developed in body text, with no attention-failure or meta-awareness literature cited

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: not treated; zero occurrences anywhere in the extraction

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: not treated; the review has no boredom-state or boredom-trait instrument or discussion

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: quantitative online questionnaire (Alfalah 2018) and semi-structured interview transcripts (Fransson et al. 2020), both surveyed within the review's own text rather than administered by Lin et al. themselves
measures.apparatus: Alfalah (2018): online questionnaire distributed to IT teachers, assessing perceptions of VR-training impact; Fransson et al. (2020): semi-structured interviews with teachers on head-mounted-display VR implementation challenges
measures.sampleN: Alfalah (2018): N=30 IT teachers; Fransson et al. (2020): N=28 teachers
measures.keyResult: Alfalah (2018): technology training 'may be maximized for the integration of VR technology' (direct quote, ~p.7); Fransson et al. (2020): teachers report a technological threshold/learning curve in operating VR equipment and software, affecting effective classroom use (~p.7). These are the review's only two explicitly sampled/instrumented sources out of 33; the remaining 31 are cited only for conceptual or review-level claims

readings.claim: VR promotes cognitive engagement through immersive, self-directed learning: immersive VR aids comprehension of complex/abstract knowledge (Papanastasiou et al. 2019), encourages self-directed inquiry via scenario reenactment (Pellas 2016), and benefits at-risk students -- including those with learning difficulties and anxiety disorders -- through personalized, adaptive environments (Maples-Keller et al. 2017).
readings.stance: asserts (synthesized across three cited primary/review sources)

readings.claim: VR's effect on behavioral engagement is contested within the review itself: positive-participation findings (Pirker and Dengel 2021; Sun and Peng 2020; Rzanova et al. 2023; Freina and Ott 2015; Wong et al. 2010; Allcoat and Von Muhlenen 2018) are set against negative-absorption findings (Cheng et al. 2015; Greenwald et al. 2018; Makransky et al. 2019) and a virtual/real-world transfer-gap caveat (Makransky and Petersen 2021).
readings.stance: qualifies (internal debate, not adjudicated by the review)

readings.claim: VR promotes affective engagement via emotional and interactive experience: VR contexts teach communication/emotion-management skills and foster empathy in children with emotional impairments (Schutte and Stilinovic 2017); enable affective interaction with virtual characters, including language-learning oral practice (Wu et al. 2013; Yuen et al. 2011; Dhimolea et al. 2022); and deepen engagement with literary material via role-play (Misak 2018).

Three challenges recur across the reviewed literature: the education system's difficulty keeping pace with VR development (Islam et al. 2015; Zhong 2017; Sahlberg 2016); heightened demands on student digital literacy (Reddy et al. 2020; Tsivitanidou et al. 2021; Necci et al. 2015; Farmer and Farmer 2023; Andone et al. 2018); and teachers' insufficient VR proficiency (Abich et al. 2021; Jensen and Konradsen 2018; Fransson et al. 2020).

Teacher training is proposed as the primary remedy to the teacher-proficiency challenge: Alfalah (2018), surveying 30 IT teachers, reports that technology training 'may be maximized for the integration of VR technology.'
readings.stance: asserts (proposed intervention, answering the review's third research question)

readings.claim: The review's own stated limitations qualify all findings: a small literature base, only three databases searched (Google, Scopus, Elsevier, flagged for future expansion to PubMed/Web of Science), a recency bias against very recently published articles (e.g., Rzanova et al. 2023), and a generalizability caveat from the inclusion/exclusion criteria.

Most of the 33 reviewed items are themselves reviews or conceptual introductions rather than primary empirical studies reporting original measurement data; only Alfalah (2018) and Fransson et al. (2020) carry an explicit sample size in Lin et al.'s own text, meaning this 'critical review' is substantially a review of reviews.
readings.stance: qualifies (this entry's own meta-level observation, not stated by the authors)

concepts.term: PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)

interlocutors.name: Wang, M.T., & Degol, J. (2014) -- Staying engaged: knowledge and research need in student engagement
interlocutors.role: source of the cognitive/behavioral/affective tripartite engagement model organizing the entire review; most-cited article in the reviewed corpus (450 citations)

interlocutors.name: Grant, M.J., & Booth, A. (2009) -- A typology of reviews
interlocutors.role: definitional source for 'critical review' as a method, quoted directly

interlocutors.name: Moher, D., Liberati, A., Tetzlaff, J., & Altman, D.G. (2009) -- PRISMA statement
interlocutors.role: source of the PRISMA screening procedure used to select the final 33 articles

interlocutors.name: Papanastasiou, G., Drigas, A., Skianis, C., Lytras, M., & Papanastasiou, E. (2019)
interlocutors.role: cited finding: immersive VR aids comprehension of complex/abstract knowledge, supporting cognitive engagement

interlocutors.name: Pellas, N. (2016)
interlocutors.role: cited finding: VR encourages self-directed inquiry and scenario reenactment, supporting cognitive engagement

interlocutors.name: Maples-Keller, J.L., Bunnell, B.E., Kim, S.-J., & Rothbaum, B.O. (2017)
interlocutors.role: cited finding: VR's personalized/adaptive environments benefit at-risk students (learning difficulties, anxiety disorders), supporting cognitive engagement

interlocutors.name: Pirker, J., & Dengel, A. (2021)
interlocutors.role: cited finding, directly quoted, that 3-D VLE learning tasks foster intrinsic motivation and engagement; supports the positive side of the behavioral-engagement debate

interlocutors.name: Cheng, M.-T., Chen, J.-H., Chu, S.-J., & Chen, S.-Y. (2015); Greenwald, S.W., Corning, W., Funk, M., & Maes, P. (2018); Makransky, G., Terkildsen, T.S., & Mayer, R.E. (2019)
interlocutors.role: cited counter-findings supporting the negative side of the behavioral-engagement debate (absorption into the virtual world at the expense of real-life tasks)

interlocutors.name: Makransky, G., & Petersen, G.B. (2021) -- The cognitive-affective model of immersive learning
interlocutors.role: cited caveat: a persistent gap between virtual-environment learning experiences and real-world knowledge transfer

interlocutors.name: Schutte, N.S., & Stilinovic, E.J. (2017)
interlocutors.role: cited finding: VR fosters empathy and communication/emotion-management skills in children with emotional impairments, supporting affective engagement

interlocutors.name: Reddy, P., Sharma, B., & Chaudhary, K. (2020)
interlocutors.role: source of the digital-literacy definition, directly quoted, used to frame the digital-literacy challenge

interlocutors.name: Jensen, L., & Konradsen, F. (2018)
interlocutors.role: cited finding on teachers needing production/editing ability for head-mounted-display content, supporting the teacher-proficiency challenge

interlocutors.name: Fransson, G., Holmberg, J., & Westelius, C. (2020)
interlocutors.role: primary interview study (N=28 teachers) on operational/technological VR barriers, one of only two explicitly sampled sources in the review

interlocutors.name: Alfalah, S.F. (2018)
interlocutors.role: primary questionnaire study (N=30 IT teachers), directly quoted, proposing teacher training as the remedy to the proficiency challenge

interlocutors.name: Islam, N., Beer, M., & Slack, F. (2015); Zhong, L. (2017); Sahlberg, P. (2016)
interlocutors.role: cited findings supporting the education-system-pace challenge

interlocutors.name: Misak, J. (2018)
interlocutors.role: cited finding on VR role-play in virtual literature and meta-cognition; the review's only (thin) touchpoint with an attentional/meta-awareness-adjacent construct

tensions.axis: VR's effect on student behavioral engagement: positive-participation reading (Pirker and Dengel 2021; Sun and Peng 2020; Rzanova et al. 2023; Freina and Ott 2015; Wong et al. 2010; Allcoat and Von Muhlenen 2018) vs. negative-absorption reading (Cheng et al. 2015; Greenwald et al. 2018; Makransky et al. 2019), further qualified by a virtual/real transfer-gap caveat (Makransky and Petersen 2021)
tensions.note: the review states plainly that 'there is debate about whether VR has a positive impact on student behavioral engagement' but resolves it only by noting that 'these complexities and diversities' must be taken into account, without adjudicating between the two readings.

tensions.axis: the review's broad three-question framing vs. its self-acknowledged narrow evidentiary base (three databases; small literature set; recency-biased citation counts)
tensions.note: the authors themselves flag that their inclusion/exclusion criteria and limited database search 'might have limited the generalizability of the results,' an internal tension between the review's stated scope and its actual evidentiary depth that this entry also independently observes via Table 1 (most reviewed items are themselves reviews, not primary studies).

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- engagement self-report channel
dataset_channels.note: Wang and Degol's (2014) cognitive/behavioral/affective tripartite engagement construct, or a derivative short-form self-report instrument, offers a plausible engagement/self-report channel for the not-yet-built VR Attention Study dataset entry, complementing rather than duplicating that entry's likely physiological (EEG/eye-tracking) channels; unconfirmed until the dataset entry specifies its own instrumentation and whether it adopts an engagement self-report measure at all (P/anticipatory-application).
